utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [redacted] And I put the phone down, and then I informed the SUP. I informed the fire-fighting service and got dressed very quickly, and I went to the shop. And when I arrived at the shop, the gentlemen from the police station were already there, as well as the firefighters. So they took over the case. At 7.30 only, when the technical service came from the town of Doboj, they disarmed the explosives. And there is a report about this at the SUP.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for that. I just want to clarify one aspect of your answer. [redacted]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [redacted]. I'm not clear if you mean that you should leave the dynamite there or whether it was being suggested that you leave the store. Do you understand? Can you please clarify that aspect of your answer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. He just said that dynamite was placed [redacted] [redacted], and he meant that I should do something,

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps it was some well-meaning citizen who wanted me to at least save something, because I had suffered some damage several months before.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps I need to clarify one further aspect [redacted]. About when was -- did this dynamite incident occur [redacted] [redacted]?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, this was sometime in the month of March 1992.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: This happened sometime at around 10.30 or -- 8.30 or 9.00 in the

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: firefighters came as well in their fire truck. We took all possible steps so that the fire truck would get as close as possible [redacted] [redacted]. This happened, as far as I can recall, sometime in October or November of 1991. [redacted]

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I reported it to the police, and the police came several times to that location. They made a report. [redacted] [redacted]. But they were so busy with many such other cases, because things like this occurred several times per week, so that they couldn't manage to process each of these cases, and they couldn't find out who were the people who were committing this. Frequently, when I went to town, I would hear from my fellow citizens that either their shop was burnt down or blown up or some power lines for electricity or weekend houses were also destroyed. As far as I understood it, they had too much work and there were too many cases to deal with, including my case. I didn't get any results. And I tried to find out as soon as possible who did this, because I never harmed anybody. I engaged a lawyer privately. [redacted]. As far as I know, he worked at the SUP in Tuzla. Because we had those changes in 1990 or 1991, he probably saw that it was better for his business to work privately, so he opened a private office. So I engaged him, and he was working on that case until the 17th of April, 1992. On two occasions I met with him, once near Tuzla and once in the centre of the town of Modrica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this gentleman's occupation properly described as that of lawyer or was it something else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, most probably. Since he had such an office, he probably did have some such profession. He was a criminal inspector.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. And did he carry out an investigation [redacted] [redacted] into who had committed those acts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, he did, because it was mutually beneficial for me to gain the information for him to earn some money in return. He asked for an advance from me twice. Once I gave him, as far as I remember -- and I have a receipt somewhere. So I gave him 200 marks once, and the next time I gave him 600 German marks. The second time that we met in the centre of town of Modrica, there were several of us because I had requested that. I was afraid that I wouldn't get adequate information but that I would give the money for it. So I brought my wife with me, and I took one of my fellow citizens. His name is Sulejman Tihic. He worked as a public prosecutor at the time in the town of Modrica. I also want to add that for a while, he worked as a public prosecutor, but at that time he was a lawyer with a private practice. So in the presence of these persons [redacted], whom I mentioned before, he told me that there are all the indications that this was committed by Fadil Topcagic and Igor Rukavina, my fellow citizens from my town, but he asked us to keep this quiet until he forwards all the documents to the official SUP authorities in my town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he ever get an opportunity to do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time then, the war happened to break out in Bosnia and Herzegovina and in my town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Was your case - and I'm referring to the case of the [redacted] - ever commented upon in the press?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Sometime at the beginning of 1992, an article appeared in a [redacted]. [redacted]. And there was a photograph and also an article on one page, with the general -- I cannot tell you the general sense of the whole article, word by word, but it went something like this: In Bosanski Samac, there's been another burning and another explosion on such-and-such a date. [redacted]

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Somebody was quoted as saying -- and there was a comment between the journalist and that person at the Palma restaurant, across the street from the courthouse in my town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was the person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Borislav Pisarevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I just want to be clear about what the comment was. It was -- the comment was that there had been [redacted] [redacted]?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. It's been translated properly. That was the general sense of the article. And it was also added that one helmet was found in there, which was a souvenir, and also some bullets, which were also souvenirs. Other than that, there was nothing else. There were three bullets and a helmet, souvenir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Can you remember anything else about the newspaper article, or is that the extent of your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. di Fazio. Can we get a clarification as to how the helmet and the bullets were souvenirs? MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Souvenirs of what? MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. I'll clarify that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you heard Her Honour's question. Can you explain what you mean when you say that there were --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- reports of bullets and helmets as souvenirs? That's what's a little puzzling.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I called it a souvenir, but my son, whose name is such-and-such --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Don't mention --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- was close to the village of Crkvina, three or four days. His car had broken down in front of an inn. The inn was called Vegas. And the owner of that inn was Trile. So his car broke down while there. At that time, there were columns of tanks from Croatia and Slovenia full of our soldiers, the JNA. The forces of the JNA were withdrawing probably from the front. So according to what he said, everybody was throwing down from those trucks and tanks their helmets, their weapons, their ammunition. So he got this helmet and those three bullets. [redacted]

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I saw that the next day and the day after, I was not in favour of that; I was opposed to it, and I was waiting for a reason to get rid of that. However, this burning happened at that time, sometime in the month of October or November - I can't remember - so that when they were searching, because they had been given an assignment to do that, I gave them the keys so they could search the premises. [redacted]

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: [redacted]. So during this check, as they were leaving [redacted] they set it on fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. Did the newspaper comment on the fact that the helmet and bullets were found at the [redacted] following the fire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It said that only a helmet and three bullets were found there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me again, Mr. di Fazio. If we could go back on the transcript, page 9, and the witness's response. I'm unclear, the lines 15 through to 20. The witness says: "I gave them the keys so that they could search the premises," but it seems that then in the last part -- the last sentence: "As they were leaving [redacted], they set it on fire." MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: So I wonder whether we could get a clarification. Witness gives "them" the keys and then "they" set it on fire. If we could find out who the "them" and the "they" are. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. I'll endeavour to clarify that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, who did you give keys to so that your premises could be searched?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if I was interpreted properly. I literally said: Had they asked me, I would have given them the key to search [redacted]. So had they asked me for the keys, I would have given them the keys to search [redacted].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, please explain who you mean by "them" and "they." To whom would you have given the keys to search [redacted]

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment, I didn't know. However, later I found out about these two persons, that they were there at that facility, and I gave their names previously.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're talking about this Fadil Topcagic and Igor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: [redacted]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [redacted]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the meantime, the police came from the town of Samac. They recorded what was to be recorded, and we saved what we managed to save. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you've explained that the bullets and helmets [redacted] were souvenirs that your son had collected and taken there. Were these bullets and helmets commented upon in the newspaper article? That's what I'd like to know.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. In the newspaper article, it said that only a helmet and three bullets were found.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the newspaper article explain that they were souvenirs or is it the case that you are now explaining to us that the truth was that they were souvenirs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: I considered it to be that way, but in the article, it did not say that they were souvenirs. And it did not say in the article how they had reached my [redacted]. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I'd like to produce into evidence and ask this witness to mark a further enlargement of P9. I understand that this -- an enlargement, a similar enlargement, was placed in evidence yesterday and marked P9G. So I suppose this would be next in sequence. And I'm going to ask the witness to mark a few points on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: I've just one more question for you. How soon after your son had got the three bullets and the helmet did you know that he kept the bullets in the house, [redacted]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps the same day or perhaps the next day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: And how long later did this fire take place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Three days later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we have the formal number for the map that the witness is going to mark?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The number is P9H. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Usher and Witness, I have a red marking pen which ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Just one more question on that for you. How old is your son, or was your son at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My son was born in 1970.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. I'm just waiting to get the -- yes. I've got it on the screen. Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I'd like you to mark a few features around the town, using the red pen. And I also have a black pen which you can use in conjunction with it. Now, first of all -- don't touch the map yet, please, Witness. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And could you please use the black pen just to write a very small number "1" next to that. So the dot and the number "1" next to the dot.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. That's fine. Good. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, can you also find on the map the location [redacted] and also mark that with a small red dot? You may have to shift the paper around to get to the point.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And now using the other black pen, can you write next to that red dot a small number "2"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: Would Mr. Usher just remain there for the next couple of questions that I need to ask.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Following the takeover of the town of Bosanski Samac on the night of the 16th and the 17th, did you subsequently visit [redacted]? Just answer me yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the 17th of April, I could not visit [redacted] [redacted].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But -- okay. You were perhaps prohibited from visiting it, but did you succeed in visiting it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I managed to go with the help of Mile Simic -- Milan Simic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll get on to that story in just a moment, but before we get there, I'd like to ask you this: On the occasion that you did manage to visit the [redacted], did you have to go through a checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. At the exit out of my town, at the crossroads, or to be more precise, of the streets that forked off. So the entrance was from the direction of Modrica. One street forked off towards the railway station and the bus station, and the other one went in the direction of the centre of town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'd just like you to mark again with a red dot on the map where the checkpoint was.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And again, would you mark next to that point where the checkpoint has been depicted a small number "3," using the other black pen.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: Okay. I've finished with the map now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Now, I want to get details now of this -- of this visit to [redacted] and the manner in which you accomplished it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [redacted]? My fellow citizens were saying that there was a checkpoint at the exit out of Samac. So I could not leave without some kind of paper. [redacted].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you solve the problem?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked how a person could get that, and the answer was given to me by [redacted] who worked with me. His name was [redacted]. That I should go to Uniglas and that I should try to get this. In Uniglas, there was some kind of an office. At that moment, I didn't know who was working there or why. So I went to the Uniglas factory at the entrance of my town in the direction of the village of Tisina. When I got there, in the hall in that building, in the factory, there were many of my fellow citizens. We were chatting amongst ourselves and asking why, which person came there, and I found out that, in that office, people could get a paper allowing them to leave town. That's what I needed too. And I was pleased to hear that. I was pleased to have gotten to the right place. Not much time went by, and Milan Simic appeared. Since we knew each other for many years, he said hello to me. He patted me on the shoulder and said, "Did you need anything, [redacted]?" [as interpreted] I started telling him about my problems, and he said, "Wait. I'll take you into the office. I'll have your name called out." And not much time went by. My name was called out at the door by Milan Simic, and my name was the first. There were many people in the hallway, many other people. Inside, I found his colleague from work. His last name was Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I just interrupt you there, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry. I have an objection to the transcript. If my learned colleague can ask again the witness to repeat what Milan Simic exactly told him, because what the witness has said is not in the transcript. MR. DI FAZIO: I can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, counsel can do that. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just tell us again what it was that Milan Simic said to you when you encountered him in the office. Just tell us the words that he said again, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Milan Simic saw me, he put his hand on my shoulder and he said, "What did you need, [redacted]?" MR. DI FAZIO: Does that solve the problem for counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Because that was exactly what the witness had said, and it was not in the transcript. Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I just want to ask you some questions about what you've already said before you go on to tell us more about this episode. First of all, how many people were gathered there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the hall, in front of the door of that office, there were about six or seven of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were their ethnic backgrounds?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now that I think back, they were all --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand the answer. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now that I think back, all of these people were of Serb ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This Uniglas office, as far as you're aware, at the time that this occurred, this visit occurred, was Mr. Milan Simic employed by them or working with them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: He never worked in that factory, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the place have a secretary or clerks working there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't notice a secretary. I didn't notice any clerks. However, at the factory, I saw many soldiers in camouflage uniforms that were working around the machines. They were doing something. This was on the second floor. And the view from there of the machines that were downstairs, where the machines were - this Uniglas, they made glass - you could see everything. You could see the entire working area of the factory. And I saw many people who were in uniform. I don't know what their assignment was, why they were in there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, were these soldiers armed or were they just in uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were not armed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know what the purpose was or what the people were seeking, that is, the Serbs, the six or seven Serbs you say who were assembled there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before I said that, through contacts with them -- I mean, while I was waiting for Milan Simic to come up, I already stated that they were waiting for passes, for movement. Some people needed to go in the direction of Brcko, some people needed to go in the direction of Bijeljina, some people needed to go in the direction of Serbia, Belgrade, things like that. I remember these conversations as if they were taking place right now. So as far as I could understand then, I came to the 8 conclusion that I could also get this paper in order to get to the [redacted] At that moment, I did not know who was working inside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you've told us that Mr. Simic appeared and patted you on the back and asked you what you needed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you eventually granted -- I'll rephrase that. Did you eventually get to see him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Soon after that, he opened the door. He called out my name. I walked in. I found his colleague from work and him. He asked me about my family, about my children. We asked each other. And then he asked me what I needed. I explained to him enough, at least to my mind, [redacted], and I didn't have to explain all of this to him in great detail. And I told him that I did not have the possibility to go there, because that was in the direction of Skarici. And also, there was a checkpoint at the exit out of my town, so there were problems. He sat at the desk --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can the witness speak slowly? MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, just slow down a bit. Slow down a bit, because your voice has to be interpreted, and the interpreters are having a hard job of it, so just slow down. There's plenty of time and you can tell us the story a bit more slowly, okay?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: So after that, when I explained to him why I had come, since we asked each other about how we were doing, he took a piece of paper, and there were several of these certificates in front of him. He wrote my name and surname on one of them, the direction of movement, and he signed it for me. We shook hands and I left that office and this factory, and I went in the direction of my house. When I got home, I told my wife about all of this. At that time my car was still in front of the house. We got into the car and we set out [redacted] When I got to the outskirts of town, that is the location of the [redacted]. The guards stopped me there and they said, "Where are you going?" These guards were my neighbours who lived there at the outskirts of Samac,

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: and I went several times during the day to that place, so I called them all neighbours. I showed them this paper and they let me go through.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: [redacted]. I suggested to my wife that we get into the car and go back, and that's exactly what we did. When we got home, we were wondering what to do and how to do all of this, [redacted] and everything, and the situation was such that obviously we could not go every day. However, the permit was unrestricted. There was not a specific date there. It said that I had the right [redacted].

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: [redacted], [redacted]. We could hardly wait for the next day.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: [redacted]. That's what we did. Well, as we were getting in and out, we would always hear this shooting at us from the direction of these back houses that were bordering on the outskirts of my town of Samac. So that is to say --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I don't actually need to know about what happened [redacted]. What I'm actually interested in is the use of the document. You were able to use the document to gain -- to get through these checkpoints on at least two occasions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. There wasn't a date on this document at all. It said my name and surname and the direction of movement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you have said that movement was prohibited. I'd like you to look at this document that I produce to you, please. MR. DI FAZIO: And for the benefit of Defence counsel, they will know of it as C12 in the list of Prosecution exhibits. I have copies for the Chamber and the registry, and it's been officially translated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can I ask you, please, to just read that document. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, it will be my intention to seek the admission of this document into evidence at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. May I hear from the Defence if there is any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are not aware of the document because we have not received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Because the Prosecution said it can be identified --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: He did --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did indeed identify it as C12, but we -- we haven't got our folders of C documents. So if we can have at least one copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: I have copies here and I'll --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. If they can -- MR. DI FAZIO: -- get --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: -- be shown to the Defence. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. Thank you. My colleague Ms. Reidy also points out that, in correspondence that we have received from the Defence, this is indicated as one of the documents that they will not be objecting to. So that might also assist -- assist the Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, have you had a chance to look at that document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have read this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The document says that exit and entry to the town is prohibited without the consent of the chief of the public security station or a person authorised by him, based on the prior authorisation of the municipal Crisis Staff of the Serbian people of Bosanski Samac in Pelagicevo. Now, do you have any knowledge of authorisation being required by the chief of the public security station or a person duly authorised by him or the municipal Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Before the witness answers -- yes. Your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Objection, Your Honours, because this is clearly speculation -- speculating, because how can witness know that? MR. DI FAZIO: With respect, it can't possibly be objectionable, because the witness may know about it. He may have heard from witnesses. He may have had contact with the Crisis Staff. I don't know. The question is certainly legitimate. The witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, I thought so. MR. DI FAZIO: -- the witness can't speculate, and if that is what Mr. Zecevic is concerned about, then of course I agree with in that respect, but the question isn't objectionable. It really depends on what the witness answers. And the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, because the witness is being asked whether he has any knowledge. MR. DI FAZIO: He may have knowledge. He may have attended a meeting, for all I know. I mean, we'll just have to hear what he says, and then the Chamber will be able to assess as to whether or not it's speculative or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I think the answer -- the question is legitimate. You can go ahead. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll just repeat the question, Witness. The document says that entry into and out of Bosanski Samac is prohibited unless you've got permission from three sources -- one of three sources; chief of the public security station, someone authorised by the chief of the public security station, or based on authorisation from the Crisis Staff. Now, do you have any knowledge of this sort of authorisation being required before you could move in and out of town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We would often hear on the Radio Serbian Samac this order. I don't know whether it said "We hereby order," or, "It is hereby ordered," but what I see in front of me now is something that circulated amongst ourselves, my fellow citizens, that you were not permitted to leave Samac. And I heard from my wife that she had heard this order or such an order on the radio. But since I had to leave the town anyway [redacted], we were concerned how we would do it and so on. But had this order not been -- had I not known about this order, I would have probably left [redacted] on my own initiative to perform all the tasks that I had to perform. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I believe it hasn't been given a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. No, because I was waiting for the Defence to look at it, and you had said that they had indicated they would have no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I first of all have to apologise. I misunderstood the question. That is why I objected. I'm sorry for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let me -- just bear me one moment, because I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Could we have the number for both the English and the translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. For the English one is P35, for the B/C/S version is P35 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One other aspect of this episode of your travelling [redacted] [redacted]that I haven't clarified is when this happened. In relation to the events of the night of the 16th and the 17th of April, when did you go [redacted] and produce the note that Milan Simic gave you and get through the checkpoint? When?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next day, I had the obligation to go to the Territorial Defence. The day after, I had the obligation to go to the furniture factory, the Budcnost factory. So this could have happened on Monday or Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Tuesday of the following week. So it was probably on the 21st or the 22nd of April.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1992. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to move to another topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Just before you do that, may I just ask the

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: permit, in other words, allowing you to travel between [redacted] your home as many times as you like, or was it just for one trip?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It didn't say how many times I was permitted to go. It only held my name, my last name, and the direction of movement. So I could have gone back and forth several times. Nobody took this permit or certificate from me. I had it with me all the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: And you did move up and down more than once?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I said earlier that I went on two occasions. The first time, I wasn't ready [redacted]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that the last time that you used it?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: Yes. That was the last time [redacted].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've told the Chamber that you had a working life involving

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [redacted]. Following the 16th and 17th of April, 1992, did you find a new line of work?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: Yes. After the 17th of April, on the radio it was broadcast for us to come so that they could make a list of the population, a census. So I mentioned this. I went to the TO building once as well, and these lists were made there. And according to these lists, work groups were made up. After that, on the 18th of April, or the 19th - I don't remember the date exactly - I went to my work obligation. My work duties comprised the following: I was digging --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness. Witness, I'll get into all of that shortly, but I need quite a bit more detail before we get to that. First of all, you -- how did you come to report for what you referred to as your work obligation?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I explained yesterday that I was at the TO building. I reported there as a conscientious citizen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And you told us that your name and details were taken. On that occasion, was anything said to you about work obligation?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: Name, last name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. And on that occasion, was anything --

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: No. No, nothing was said. MR. DI FAZIO: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: May I just -- can I call the registry assistant, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you first find out about this work obligation, and how did you find out about it?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: A courier came to my front door and informed me that I needed to come before the retired persons' building - that's what we called it, the pensioners' building, and that's where the local commune was - because of the work obligation and because there was a lot of fear. I was afraid, and so were the other citizens, so I reported -- I responded to this call. When I got to the local commune building, I met a lot of my fellow citizens there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I just --

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I just ask you to stop there. I'd like you to indicate on the map that I showed you before the location of this community hall. It's P --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: P9H. MR. DI FAZIO: P9H. Could that be produced to the witness, please. And Mr. Usher, perhaps we could use the same marking pen and black numbering pen. May I approach the witness and have a look at the map, if Your Honours please? I've forgotten the last number that we used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, my colleagues tell me that it was 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. That was the last one, 3. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Witness, can you please just indicate where the community hall was that you had to report to and mark it with a red dot, and next to that write in a small number "4."

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Counsel, we have a problem with having it on the ELMO, because then it will be shown -- the public may see it. What we can do is the witnesses can mark off the ELMO number "4" and then it can be shown around within the courtroom, rather than use the ELMO. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So you can ask him to have the map in front of him, mark it number "4," then the usher will show us all. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. I'm grateful to Your Honours. I hadn't considered that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The problem when there are protective measures is that you have all these intervening matters that you have to take care of.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's a community hall. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is a community hall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no. We are talking about the other places which --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, the other -- yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, which are already on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I understand. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Actually, Mr. di Fazio, I have a short question for yourself. I'm just wondering what is the relevance of us knowing where the community or commune hall is on the map? MR. DI FAZIO: It's not particularly relevant, if Your Honours please. I mean, it really wouldn't matter if it was in the spot indicated that the witness has placed that, or anywhere else, but it does give you background evidence of where this place was, and that's its only significance, if Your Honours please. There's no evidential point that I'm trying to score here or make.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let's continue with your narrative, Witness, please. You were telling us how you reported to the community hall and that you saw your fellow citizens there. Tell us what happened when you -- you reported, and I'm now --

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- talking about the first time, of course.

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: When I reported to the local commune, I received the task, as well as several other of my fellow citizens, to put sand into bags, to make sandbags. There was a small truck waiting for us in front of the local commune building. We got into the truck and they took us in the direction of the Silos factory, and it was part of the agricultural combine, and this is where we made sandbags all day. Other of my fellow citizens received different duties, and this is what it was like every day. Six or seven people would go in one group, and the next day it wouldn't have to necessarily be that you would be in the same group of people. And this is how things proceeded until I was detained in August.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the exact date. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll get on to your detention at a later time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You heard what the interpreter said? They didn't catch the date. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm sorry. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you just let us know the date of your arrest in August, please.

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: The 11th of August.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. When you first assembled at the community hall, can you tell us what the ethnic background of your fellow citizens who were assembled with you was?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: All those who went to forced labour were of Muslim or Croat ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just answer me briefly: Did you assemble inside the community hall or outside the community hall?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: In front of the local commune hall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just keep your answers brief. Did this assembling outside, or in front of the community hall, represent a pattern that occurred; in other words, in the following months, is that where you would normally assemble before going off to your tasks?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: Yes. Whenever I went for work obligation, I would come in front of the local commune building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see any of your fellow citizens inside the community hall?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: Yes, I did see them often. A restaurant was opened inside, where you could drink coffee or juice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who would gather there inside the community hall?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: Inside the building were mostly people - if that's what you mean - people of Serbian ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you see them there in the mornings when you assembled to be given your tasks?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: Yes. We would usually go to our work duties around 7.00 or 8.00 in the morning, and the town was, to a degree, already lively at that time. People were coming and going. And inside the restaurant as well, I would see people sitting and drinking coffee or drinking juice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see any signs or placards outside the community hall?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: Yes. A poster or a placard appeared on the door of the local commune, and this was ten or so days later. So sometime around the 27th of April a poster appeared on the door of the old pensioners' hall, and it stated: "Entry forbidden to Muslims, Croats, and dogs." This poster was there the whole day. As far as I remember, it wasn't there the next day. It had been taken down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you feel when you saw that? Please tell us.

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: It was very difficult.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to ask you questions about the general pattern of your work. First of all, I'd like you to tell the Chamber the sort of jobs that you did in between those days when you first started, shortly after the takeover, and your arrest. You've already described one task. That was the filling of sandbags. Please describe other tasks that you did.

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: Mostly I was digging trenches and I was digging bunkers when the lines changed, the separation lines changed in the direction of the village of Prud. So when we were going down towards the embankment, in that direction, we were told to dig bunkers. We were told to make those bunkers as strong as possible. One of our tasks also was to go on trucks in the direction of the Samac-Sarajevo railway line and to take the rails there and to load them into -- or to take the wooden parts of the railway line and load them onto the trucks and to reinforce the bunkers. We also mowed the grass in front of the bunkers. This is mostly what my duties were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. As far as the railway tracks are concerned, were they the wooden sleepers that go underneath the two rail tracks that you had to dig up?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes. The wooden -- the wooden parts that are placed beneath the rails.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, tell the Chamber how the wooden sleepers would be used after you had dug them up and loaded them onto trucks.

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: We would come close to the line of separation, and then four of us, or six of us, depending on how many of us were in the group, we would carry these railway sleepers and we would take them to the bunkers, and then we would place them crosswise on top of the bunkers, and then on top of that we would put some more earth in order for this bunker to be reinforced properly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were carrying out this operation, how far were you from the front line?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: You could hear shots frequently from the other side, and according to my estimate, now that I think about it, it was maybe two to three hundred metres, as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the actual trenches themselves, the actual holes in the ground, so to speak? Did you ever perform any labour digging those?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: Yes, I did, the communication trenches and trenches, and in our language it's one and the same thing. So when the lines changed, we would dig new ones, as well as after every rainfall we would repair the old ones. Because the earth was freshly dug in the direction of the line of separation, so that when it rained, all the water would come into the bunkers and it would be difficult to move because of the mud. So then I was given the task of cleaning all that out and placing it outside as a sort of parapet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do I understand from your evidence that the question of a trench is not simply a matter of digging it and that's -- once that's happened, the task is completed; it needs to be maintained, and on occasions, new ones had to be dug as the lines --

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Earlier you described how you went to the Silos factory and made sandbags. Do you know what those sandbags were used for?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us what they were used for.

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: Yes. We would load those sandbags into a truck and then use them to protect certain buildings in Samac, like the municipal building. We would also place these sandbags in front or behind windows, as a parapet. In that same building, the Silos building, another team had the task of taking them upstairs to offices somewhere. We would be filling them downstairs, another two or three men would be bringing those bags upstairs and placing them in the windows of that building where we were making the sandbags in order to make a sort of protection from bullets. Now that I remember, and when I analyse, my town seemed more like a barracks to me, a barracks that was within firing range, and also the target of other weapons, so that the separation line, the line of separation, was in the direction of the north, 300 metres away from my house, 500 metres in the direction of the east -- of the west, and in the east, two or three kilometres away, so that we lived inside as if we were exposed to constant shelling. So that these bags and these wooden sleepers were all used for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the digging of trenches and the maintenance of them all conducted in areas around the town of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: Yes. Mostly we worked around or near Bosanski Samac, but we went to other towns and neighbouring villages. And also when the town of Odzak was captured, I also went for forced labour to Odzak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll ask you about Odzak later, but I now want to ask you about transportation from the community hall to the work site, the place where you would be digging these trenches. How did you get there?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: If we were to go further, to Pisari or Zasavica, we would be taken there by truck. But if we went closer, towards the direction of the River Sava and Croatia or in the direction of the village of Prud, that was quite close. I said it was 200 to 300 metres away from the line of separation. Then we would go on foot. As we were passing by, if we were going on foot, it was very difficult to move because there were frequent checks in the town, and they were practically capturing Muslims and Croats only because their name wasn't right, and they would take them to the municipal building. And all of us citizens knew that, so that when we were going home on our way back from work, if we were on foot, then we would hide. We would walk very close to the houses. And then we would also jump over fences and go through the backyards and gardens in order to reach our homes in the least noticeable way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I just ask you briefly one last question perhaps before the morning break? When the men -- when you were taken on trucks to your work sites, were you guarded?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: Yes. There was a guard sitting in the front of the truck and also one in the back in a camouflage uniform and with a rifle. MR. DI FAZIO: Is this an appropriate time, if Your Honours please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We will have our break and resume our proceedings at 1130 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. Before my learned colleague proceeds on, I would like to inform this Honourable Trial Chamber that my client is not feeling well today and that he will waive his right of his presence in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well. He will be allowed to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You can proceed, Mr. di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. Thank you. If Your Honours please, I've gathered that the technical staff are having a bit of trouble with keeping private or confidential some portions of the evidence that might tend to identify this witness. I hadn't appreciated what I was doing, and now that I've been apprised of the situation, apparently it would be desirable for me to ask that we move into private session from time to time to avoid that problem arising.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Because it's very difficult to keep checking every word to make sure that identifying matters are not exposed to the public. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You divide up your areas of evidence, and when you feel we should go into private session, you say so. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. I -- yes. I've been set straight now, and I understand my obligation, and I apologise for any inconvenience caused to the technical staff. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, can you tell us of the conditions under which you worked? And by that, I mean the hours that you worked and the days per week that you worked.

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: Working hours usually began in the morning at 8.00, and the working day would end [as interpreted] for as long as there was daylight. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. So this evil happened on the 17th of April, 1992. In my country, this is a spring month. As the days and weeks went by, the days became longer, so as the summer came, the days would get longer and we would work throughout the day for as long as it was light. Conditions were hard. We did not have food on the ground. We had to make do, bringing things from home, bringing sandwiches. People would take whatever they had, actually, and we would share it. We would share it amongst ourselves at the place where we worked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were actually working, digging trenches or filling sandbags or cleaning out trenches, were guards, armed guards, standing around?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: Yes. These lines were always operational. Depending on the number of soldiers there, there were always guards inside with us, these soldiers who were manning the line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What sort of numbers of people would assemble at the community hall in the mornings before you went off to your different tasks?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: There would be 100 to 150 of us. Every morning we would not all get duties. Sometimes somebody would be off and could go back home. However, most people had to work. Some people went to the forest to chop wood, others would go to the agricultural farm to milk the cows. Some groups went to clean various facilities, from the glass and rubble that was there. There were groups that went to certain villages that had been taken in order to collect the remaining livestock, agricultural products as they were coming in, as various crops were getting ripe, and also to collect things at abandoned houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you comment on the ethnic background of these 100 to 150 people who would assemble in the mornings?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: All were exclusively of Serb and Muslim ethnicity. I beg your pardon; Croat and Muslim ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've spoken of having to work close to the front lines. Were you exposed - I mean you personally - were you exposed to danger, to shotgun fire or weapon fire?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. At every moment, from the 17th of April until I was released, until I was sort of set free, I was exposed to danger. While I was at home, I was exposed to danger, searches of my very own home. While I was walking from the house to the local commune, I was exposed to the danger of mistreatment and humiliation. While I worked, I was exposed to the dangers of the enemy side, while there was shooting and while there were exchanges of gunfire. Often it would happen that in front of the parapets, in front of the trenches, in front of the bunkers, we would clean the area, and an exchange of gunfire would start, and then we would lie on the ground and crawl back to the trench that we had dug previously.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: That happened several times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever have to mow grass or cut grass?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. There were situations when I had to cut grass in front of the parapets, in front of the line, in front of the communication trenches, so that those who were behind the parapet would have a better view in front of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You described some of the tasks that the assembled people had to do as collecting things from abandoned houses. Can you tell the Chamber with any more detail what precisely that meant?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: That means that when the line would shift, or when a certain village would be taken -- I can't talk about a lot of towns, because as far as I know, there is only one town that was near the place where I was. So these were mainly villages, like Garevac, Kornica, Zasavica. My local people went for work drives on trucks in order to collect goods from empty houses. Citizens who lived in those houses had fled, and then they were taking -- these other people were taking furniture, appliances, and other things that were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How would it be collected and taken away?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: It was collected in front of the house, and it was taken on trucks in the direction of Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to the material that was collected in this way?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: No. No, I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever personally engage in that particular job, collecting stuff from people's houses?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the time that you worked on the trenches or doing work associated with trenches, were any of your fellow co-workers injured or killed?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: There were such things on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what happened on those occasions, please.

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: Well, while digging in front of the trenches, my fellow citizens who were exposed to direct fire, direct gunfire and bullets, would sometimes get hit. If a person were lucky, then this person would not be hit in a vital body part and then they could survive, but then others would not survive. As far as I know, two or three men, fellow citizens of mine, got killed as they were cleaning trenches and cutting grass in front of trenches.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that something that you heard of or is that something that occurred nearby when you were actually performing the sort of work you've described?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: I heard all of that. I was not in any such team of six or seven men. However, this was so picturesque that there was one case practically in my family. A work colleague of mine who worked with me, called Galib Nurkic, had a son named Dzevad. One morning, we went in different directions to carry out our work obligation, and in the afternoon, we were informed that this son of his, Dzevad Nurkic, was killed while digging trenches. There were other such cases among my fellow citizens, but I don't know their names. But I did know that these things happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can -- I just wanted to seek clarification on this person who was killed, because we have evidence of others being killed by the guards. Now, can we have an explanation of who killed him, or how was he killed? MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You heard Her Honour's question. The Chamber wants to know how it was that Dzevad Nurkic met his death. Was it the result, as far as you're aware, of being caught in crossfire or was he killed by a guard or something like that?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: Caught in crossfire, not by a guard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the other cases that you said you heard of, were those -- were they people who were killed as a result of crossfire?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: Yes. I meant them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Just one little clarification, one little clarification. You worked on the trenches, and you said you cut the grass. I take it you cut the old growth in that area. Now, from where you were, could you visually see the front line or the soldiers, the Croat soldiers on the other side? Were they within your sight?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could not see the soldiers on the other side. However, I did see the parapets on the other said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: And how far would you estimate these parapets were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About 200 or 300 metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. di Fazio, I just wonder in terms of the translation. Page 39, line 13, concerning the death of the son of the witness's co-worker. The sentence reads: "However, this was so picturesque" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note: It is a literal translation of what the witness said. It sounds the same way in the original language as it does in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you, Interpreter, but I still don't understand what the meaning is that the witness is trying to convey. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm none the wiser either, if Your Honours please. I'll see what I can do to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, Their Honours are just concerned about one particular expression that you used. We want to be clear and we want to understand it. You said that you were not a team of six or seven men and, "... this was so picturesque," picturesque, "that there was one case practically in my family." And we're not sure what you mean by that word "picturesque." Can you just tell us what you meant to say, what you meant to convey, the meaning of what you --

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: I wished to say that my colleague was so close to me.

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: [redacted]. When he was killed, I was very sorry, and I commiserated with him. He was only 20 years old.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you for the clarification. I think maybe we just forget the English version of what the word means. MR. DI FAZIO: I respectfully don't think it's going to matter much in the overall picture, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were also asked about the distance and the parapets that you could see. Could you see tracer fire coming across the river towards where you were working?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: I never worked during the night. As far as I know, a tracer bullet can be seen only during the night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that when you were working during the day and you heard gunfire, you wouldn't know where the gunfire was being directed at?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: No. No. We didn't know what was being shot at and where it was coming from. If somebody did not lie down before you did, you'd say, "Lie down." So we would lie down and we would crawl in a certain direction. If we were in front of the parapet, then we would crawl away in order to hide in the communication trenches and the bunkers. And if we were in the bunker up there or if we were finishing moving the earth, whatever, then we would also jump into the trenches so that we would protect ourselves from bullets, from gunfire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doing the best you can, about how many people did you hear of being killed in the way that you've described, between April and August when you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: I think that I said two or three men. Several persons were wounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You've described to the Chamber the fact of being guarded by the work site when you were digging trenches and also on the trucks when you were being taken out to the places you had to work at. Can you tell us who was guarding you? And in particular, I'd like to know if they were locals.

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: So in the morning when we would get to the local commune, in the morning at 8.00, we would get our work schedule from the gentleman who worked there at the local commune. He would read this out to us, what the groups were that were supposed to be sent to do particular work. We would then separate in front of that building. That is to say, if you were going a bit further off, then you would have a truck waiting for you there, with a driver and guards, locals. They were familiar with the terrain and they knew where you were supposed to be taken to, on this truck, that is. However, if we were going somewhere nearby, then we would be escorted by a local guard, again a person who would be familiar with the terrain, and that person would take you to the very spot. When we would get to the very spot, then his task was not to guard us. He would hand us over to these soldiers who were in the trenches. They were the ones who gave us assignments as to what we should do, whether we should repair or clean the trench or build a new bunker --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who were the soldiers --

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: -- or if some grass should be cut in front of the trenches or if it should be cleaned. And most of the soldiers in the trenches were locals of Serb ethnicity. Here and there, there were some persons that I didn't know, who were not from my town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of a body called the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: Yes, I heard of the 4th Detachment sometime at the end of 1992 -- 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter correction. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to know if any of the men who were guarding you or transporting you on the trucks were members of the 4th Detachment, as far as you're aware.

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: Now that I go back to it and think about it, since it's a small town, it was known who was a member of the 4th Detachment even before the war. During the war, as far as I know, many of those people who were issued with weapons and went to firing practice, shooting practice before the war were members of the Serbian army during the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And what I'd like to know is: Did you ever see any members of the 4th Detachment guarding you, either on the way to your work locations or at the work locations? That's what I'd like to know.

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: Yes, I did. After the 17th of April, the 4th Detachment wasn't so important, and I don't know any more whether it was even called the 4th Detachment. After the 17th of April 1992, it was called the Serbian army. As far as I know, the 4th Detachment became or merged into the Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the soldiers at the front who actually handed out the tasks in respect of trenches, as far as you're aware, were any of those members of the 4th Detachment? I'm not talking about the guards on the truck or the guards who escorted you; I'm talking about the soldiers who were at the trenches once you arrived and who assigned tasks in respect of the trenches.

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: Yes, I did notice. It's difficult for me to recall the names. We in Samac used to know each other more by our nicknames, so that I know all of the neighbours, my close neighbours who were close [redacted] [redacted]. The people that I addressed as neighbours, they were in those trenches that we dug and cleaned and maintained. Yes, they were in those trenches.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And if I understand correctly, your position is this: In respect of the soldiers who were in the trenches engaged in warfare, a number of them, as far as you could tell, were in the Serb army, and secondly, were locals. Is that a fair assessment of your position?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: Yes. That is also what I thought. So locals, my fellow citizens, did used to go to those exercises of the 4th Detachment and were issued with weapons, and they were in the trenches after the 17th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those men occasionally gave you orders in respect of tasks at the trenches, at the trench locations?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, all this work that you were doing, did you ever get paid for it?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: Never. I never received a single dinar, not even one kilo of bread. During the period from the 17th of April, 1992 until the 11th of August, 1992, I never received one single thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During that very same period, did you ever see any of your co-workers receiving money or pay?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: This is the first time that I'm hearing of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During that same period, did you ever hear, was it ever reported to you, that co-workers were receiving pay?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: No. I never heard, nor did anybody ever draw my attention to the fact that anyone received any kind of compensation for the work obligation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Or during that same period, did anybody promise that all of you would be paid for the work that you were doing at some time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. MR. DI FAZIO: Can the witness please be shown Exhibit D22E/2 ter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, Witness, do you read Cyrillic?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I learnt it at school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The document has a number of columns. MR. DI FAZIO: Would Your Honours just bear with me for one minute, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. I withdraw that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The document speaks for itself. It has a list of names, total days, and total sum, in three columns. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it purportedly applies to the months of April, May, June, July, August of 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: Yes. That's also what I see. It is a list of workers, and that is before me now, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And I would be grateful if you would read out the title of the document into the transcript so we can have that clarified at least, please. The title at the top of the document, page 1.

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: "List of workers engaged in the work brigade for the months of April, May, June, July, August 1992." MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I think this evidence would be the sort of evidence that requires private session, because some names will be mentioned that are linked to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, we can move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've told us all about the work conditions. I want to ask you about other aspects of life in Bosanski Samac between April and August 1992. You touched upon the question of searches of your home. Can you tell the Chamber if, in those months, your home was searched, by whom, and how often?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: Several times; from the first days, all the way up to when I was brought into custody. When I was brought into custody, that was the last time that the house was searched. They were looking around houses. I don't even know myself any more what they were looking for, but they were always stating that they were looking for radio transmitters, weapons. They would always close us off in part of the premises and a guard would always remain with us with a rifle on the ready, and two others would search the house, and they would search drawers, cupboards, the bathrooms, pantries, the attic. That's the kind of house I had. These people were not from the territory of Samac. As far as I know, there were several such groups, led by persons unknown to me. But I found out from other citizens that one group was led by a man called Laki, that one group was led by a man called Zvjezdan, and there was another group led by a man called Teri. In these groups, there were usually two to three men respectively. Usually when they would come to my place, there would always be three men. During the first days, they searched my house several times, and as time went by, they would come once in 10 to 15 days and then they would order us to sit down, either in a chair or on a couch. One of them would be guarding us and two would search the house. This was painful. However, they never mistreated me physically.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Was your house ever searched by any other men or was it always the same group that would come?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: It would always be different groups. So I remembered one group, led by Laki. He came on several occasions. However, I had lots of searches. I can't remember the exact number. He did not always lead that group, and he was not always a member of that group either.
