utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were the searches conducted; at night or during the day?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: During the day I wasn't at home most of the time, so they did not come. However, when the curfew would start, then they would come, during the night. This would happen at 11.00 or 12.00, at 3.00, after midnight. You would have to open up when they would knock at the door so that they could get in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your last answer raises one last issue on the question of your work obligation. You've told us of the hours of work that you did, but how often per week would you have to perform your work obligation in the trenches and so on?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: I don't know. In this period, from the 17th of April until the 11th of August, 1992, was I off perhaps three or four times? So four to five days I got time off, and I was working during all the rest of these days, every day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Weekends included?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: Weekends included. War was waged during weekends too. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I know it's one minute --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. MR. DI FAZIO: I know it's one minute to 1.00, but could we break here? I realise there's one last topic on forced labour that I need to complete before I move into general conditions, and this would be an appropriate moment in the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. Yes. We'll continue the proceedings in the afternoon at 1530 hours. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.59 p.m. 24 25

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Prosecution is continuing. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Earlier in your evidence, you mentioned going to Odzak in the context of this work obligation. I'd like to ask you about that. Firstly, can you recall when you went to Odzak?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. The first day when I left for Odzak was the 17th of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had there recently been any military action in the area, that is, around the 17th of July, 1992?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: In 1992, on the 17th of July, 1992, the next town to us to the west, which is 20 kilometres away, was captured by the Serb army in the fighting. I and ten of my fellow citizens, in the morning, received the job in the morning in front of the local commune to go in the truck of the Serbian army with a soldier in the front and in the back of the truck to go to the town to help in the cleaning and the sorting out of some facilities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. May I just interrupt to ask you this: You've referred to the next town 20 kilometres away. I'd like to be clear. Is that Odzak? Is that the town that you refer to?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: Yes. I'm speaking of Odzak. On that day, the 17th of July, we were told to go to the town of Odzak to help in the cleaning. More specifically, to clean the SUP building, because the town was deserted or abandoned by the soldiers of the Croatian and Muslim ethnicity. As far as I know, that was one of the first days after the Serb soldiers entered the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived, did you see any evidence or signs of recent fighting?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: Yes, I did. There were many animals who were upset and were just running about on the streets, in the parks, all around. There were a lot of killed animals on street which had just been pushed to the side. There were a lot of shattered windows in the town. The whole town of Odzak was teeming with Serbian soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what task did you start upon once you arrived in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: Six of us men and four women were instructed to clean the SUP building which was in the centre of Odzak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many days did you stay in Odzak engaged in this task?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: I went on two occasions, on the 17th and the 18th of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't stay overnight. You returned to Bosanski Samac and then returned back the next day. Is that a correct assessment?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: Yes. You understood me properly. I never did have the misfortune to have a spend the night out in the field. I would always return home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you been to Odzak before the war began? Were you familiar with the town and its environs?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: Yes. I had a lot of friends in Odzak, and I often used to go to shop in Odzak, and I was familiar with the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the town have a mosque?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: Yes, right next door to the SUP building which we were instructed to clean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you first arrived in Odzak to start your task of cleaning up the SUP building, was the mosque standing?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: When we arrived at Odzak, we were ordered to leave the truck, so Serb soldiers were already deployed there. We were told to go into the SUP building and to carry out the task, which I will explain later. I saw that there was a mosque next to the SUP building, and it was -- the building -- the mosque was perfectly all right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to ask you about the mosque in just a moment, but before I do so, I want to be absolutely clear about something. You say that the town was teeming with Serb soldiers. Do I take it from that that the Serb soldiers were in absolute control of the town?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: Yes. It means that they had complete control of the town. Some were leaving the town with loaded tractors, full of goods. These goods were, for example, furniture, TV sets, bicycles, different kinds of engines, anything that could be loaded on the truck and carried away. So some of them were leaving Odzak with these goods, while others were entering Odzak in columns. As I arrived from the direction of Modrica, I could see that they were -- they, Serbian soldiers, were coming in in columns. They were wearing camouflage uniforms and they were armed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In the time that you stayed in Odzak, did you see any destruction or damage caused to the mosque? Just answer me yes or no.

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: Yes. I saw that the mosque was destroyed on the 17th of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm not quite sure. Was that the first or the second day you were there?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: The first day we were on work duty, the first time that I went to Odzak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: Can the witness be shown P14A, please, and in particular, photograph 9.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, would you please have a look at that photograph and tell me if you can tell us if, first of all, that's in Odzak.

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: I assume that this is the location where the mosque used to stand in the town of Odzak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I'd just like to ask you about your last answer. You say you assume that. The Court has to be sure if you know whether that is the location. Just have a good look at the photograph. Feel free to look at it. It's on your right. You don't have to look at the TV screen. Have a close look at the photograph and tell us if you can speak with any certainty or whether you assume that is the -- whether you are merely assuming that that's the location, okay?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: On the photograph, on my right side there is the SUP building. That's where it should be, on the right side. And this building straight ahead that has foil on the windows, plastic, this is the house of my friend, a veterinarian, Adnan Cizmic, who inherited that house from his father-in-law and his wife.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the vacant block, is that where the mosque stood once?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: That is the place where the mosque used to stand. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. I've finished with the photograph, Mr. Usher. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I'd like you to tell us of the circumstances in which the mosque was destroyed. You've told us that you were at work cleaning the SUP and that it was destroyed on the first day. Please take the story from there. Tell us how it happened.

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: We were almost at the end of our job which was given to us, as men, in the SUP building. This was around 12.00 or 12.30 of that day. We were told by Serbian soldiers to go down into the cellar of the SUP building and to take shelter there, because in our immediate vicinity, the mosque was blown up by Muslims and Croats. Explosives were placed under the mosque, at the mosque. So they were trying to disarm these explosives, and there was a possibility that we might be hurt. When we heard that, we ran downstairs. I didn't even know that there was a shelter in that building. When we went downstairs, that's when I saw it. We didn't even manage to close the door. When four or five Serbian soldiers appeared at the door - because they also had the intention of taking shelter in the same place - when they came in, they were surprised to see us down there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to know the names, please, of these Serbian soldiers who appeared and took shelter with you.

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: These were my fellow citizens. One of them was called Simo Zaric. Together with him there was Toso Tutnjevic, also Savo Popovic, and also Ninkovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think I understand you, but I just need to be absolutely clear. You say one of them was called Simo Zaric. Is that the same Simo Zaric that you identified yesterday in court?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, the same Simo Zaric, [redacted].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to know with some detail, please, how events transpired in the shelter. Can you recall any of the conversation that occurred, if any?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: Yes. There was a conversation. Since we were all from the same town, they asked us what we were doing there. And I, out of the ten of us, told him that we were there to help the Serbian soldiers to clean the town of Odzak and the SUP building. And I started to explain our tasks to him in detail, and he just said, "Very well. Very well." He had a flashlight in his hand, and he kept turning it in our direction. Not long afterwards, we could hear or we could sense the ground shaking. We felt a tremor. After three or four minutes of this tremor, we opened the door, and as we did that, dust rushed in. We closed the door again for another minute or two and opened it again even though the dust hadn't settled yet. So we went outside into the yard of the SUP building, using the stairs, all of us together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you went outside, was the mosque still standing?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: The mosque should have been on my left side, but it was no longer there. All the pieces of the building and the minaret were flung everywhere, in a radius of 500 metres. There was a lot of rubble everywhere around the SUP building and in the yard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The explanation that was given to you by the Serb soldiers was that the building had been mined by Croats and Muslims. Is that the effect of your evidence?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: Yes. That is what I said and that is what I meant to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the time that you worked at the SUP building in those two days in Odzak, did any other buildings suffer the same sort of fate as the mosque?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: During those two days that I was there, no other buildings had the same fate as the mosque. According to what my fellow citizens said, if I remember well, on the 27th of July, ten days later, in 1992, the Croatian church was blown up, which was right next to the hotel in the centre of town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Odzak?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: In Odzak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. di Fazio, I'd like the witness to clarify something concerning the participation of the Muslims and Croats mining the mosque. Would the witness be able to tell us who it was thought placed the explosives under the mosque? Who placed the explosives? MR. DI FAZIO: Well, I'll certainly ask that if Your Honour pleases. I gather from his evidence that he wouldn't know, but I'll certainly ask the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Because I'm just a little bit confused, because -- I haven't got that bit of the transcript here on the screen in front of me, but what the witness said seemed to imply, in my understanding of it, that there were explosives under the mosque, and the Muslims and the Croats were trying to defuse those explosives and, as a consequence, the mosque blew up. MR. DI FAZIO: No. My understanding is this, if Your Honour pleases: He was taken downstairs by the Serbian soldier. The Serbian soldier told him that the mosque had been mined, had been mined by the Muslims and Croats, the defeated Muslims and Croats who had been sent out of the city or militarily moved, had lost, but that the building had been mined by them, by the defeated Croats and Muslims. The truth of that is something that the Prosecution will be addressing the Chamber on. It's -- you can imagine what the Prosecution's submission is going to be on that particular issue. Does Your Honour follow me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I certainly follow you, Mr. di Fazio. It's just that the witness did not say the defeated Muslims and Croats. You're adding that in. I just wouldn't mind if, if you would, to ask the witness just to say -- MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: -- to answer the question again, basically. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps you heard Her Honour's inquiry and that's something I would like to clarify with you now. I understood your evidence to be that when you arrived in the town of Odzak, that it was teeming with Serbian soldiers and that the Croats and Muslims had been defeated. Their armies and fighters had been defeated and sent out, ejected from the town of Odzak. Is that a correct assessment?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: Yes. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Now, when you were taken downstairs to seek shelter, the Serbian soldier who accompanied you told you that this building next door had been mined, mines had been placed in the building by the retreating Croat and Muslims forces. Is that the effect -- is that a correct understanding of what the Serbian soldier told you?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: Yes. That day, that is the information that I received, and that is what I meant to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Did you believe the Serbian soldier, that the defeated Croat and Muslim soldiers had mined --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Objection. Speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic. Yes. Mr. di Fazio, the objection is sustained. MR. DI FAZIO: Perhaps stretching matters there, if Your Honour pleases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I think, Mr. di Fazio, I would have preferred if you would just let the witness say what happened again rather than leading him through it. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. Yes. I'll bear that in mind in the future, if Your Honour pleases. Has the topic been clarified for Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: No, no. I understand now. It was just that the words "defeated," "retreating" were not the words that came from the witness. MR. DI FAZIO: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you also mentioned in your evidence the -- that you had been informed that the Catholic church had also been destroyed in the town of Odzak. Did you know what the location of the Catholic church -- where it was in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: Yes, I know. In the centre of Odzak, right next to the hotel, across from the Beograd department store. MR. DI FAZIO: Could the witness be shown another photograph, please, photograph number 10 from Exhibit P14A.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, would you please have a look at that photograph and tell us if you recognise the location it depicts. Only tell us if you know. Don't tell us anything that you assume, okay?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: Yes. Here on the left side was the hotel building, and behind my back was the department store, and in front of me, the building that is destroyed is the Croatian church, which was standing on the 17th and the 18th of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Can you please use the pointer and show us. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Use the metal pointer --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps -- just use the --

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: The hotel, the department store, the yard of the church, and the place where the church was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. How did you feel once you saw the mosque reduced to rubble?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: I felt uncomfortable, because I was a member of the Muslim faith. I didn't like it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you emerged from the cellar or the place that you had taken refuge in, did anyone say or comment -- say anything or comment on the sight that greeted them?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: No. No. We didn't comment about the tremor of the ground in the shelter. We didn't comment either amongst ourselves or with the Serbian soldiers, but we commented in a silent way by just keeping our heads down, the ten of us, about what had happened, and I mean the ten of us who were there to carry out our work obligation. We commented on it amongst ourselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to the destruction of the mosque and while you were still working in the SUP, had you seen any Sappers or soldiers involved in trying to remove mines from the mosque?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: No. No, I didn't see, because my task was to clean the glass and the papers that were strewn about, also to clean human faeces, and also there were two dead dogs there. There was lots of rubble there. We did not make any comments about the Sappers, I nor the other people there, and we didn't see them either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's go back to Bosanski Samac, and I want to ask you some more questions about the conditions of life there. Was there ever a curfew imposed?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: A curfew was imposed on the first day, the 17th of April. It was broadcast on the radio, the Serb radio.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the conditions of the curfew?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: It was not allowed to walk about in the month of April from 8.00 p.m. until 5.00 a.m. As time went by, the days got longer, and in this summer period, this curfew was imposed from 2200 hours until 5.00 a.m. We did not have the right to walk about during the curfew hours, while citizens of Serb ethnicity did have the right to walk about. Often I would hear commotion, men and women passing in the street, but I did not dare watch through the window, because that was forbidden.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From your home, were you able to see if the lights were on in neighbouring flats and apartments?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: Yes. I could see in the building right next door to me. There were about 50 apartments there in two buildings. I would often see lights on in those houses. Not all the windows were dark, although the order was that all the windows had to be kept dark. Often there would be power cuts, and then while electricity would come back, the windows had to have blinds drawn on them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any idea of the ethnic background of the occupants of the houses whose lights shone?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: Serb ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have lights on in your home?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: Yes, but blinds or curtains had to be drawn on the windows.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did this curfew last?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: Until I was detained. After that, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any prohibition against the gathering of people in the town?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, there was a prohibition against the gathering of more than three persons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that apply to all people or was it selective?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: It was selective; that is to say, three Muslims, or two Muslims and one Croat. People like that could not assemble in one place. Whoever did not abide by this could be taken into custody at the SUP and never return home after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you become aware of this prohibition?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: This prohibition was read over the radio, Serb Radio Samac. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I want to produce a document to the witness. The Defence will know it. It is document C80 in the Prosecution's list of exhibits. Copies have been provided to them. I have copies for the Chamber, for the Registry. I'd ask that -- it's my intention to seek the full admission of this document into evidence. Perhaps the Chamber can look at it first. I don't know if the Defence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And we have English translation for it? MR. DI FAZIO: Oh, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Any objection from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: None, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we have the numbering, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. For the English version, it's P40. For the B/C/S version, it's P40 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we have the title? MR. DI FAZIO: "Order prohibiting the gathering of three or more Muslims or Croats."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have a look at this document, please, Witness. It's probably a little hard to read, but do your best, please. The document speaks for itself. It's apparently signed by Stevan Todorovic, and it appears to be dated the 4th of August, 1992 and prohibits the gathering of three or more Muslims in public places. What I want to know is this: Is it your position that this prohibition contained in this document actually applied prior to August of 1992?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: Yes. This prohibition was in force, and I heard of it through the media. I never had this in my hands.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I appreciate that. I understand that. But my question is this: The document says that it's prohibited for that sort of gathering, but it's dated August 1992. Is it your position that a prohibition against the gathering of small groups of Muslims or Croats applied before, before, August of 1992?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: Yes, that is my opinion, because I abided by that prohibition for a long time while I was still seemingly free. For a long time I abided by that, and it was in force a lot earlier. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Mr. Usher. I've finished with the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said that you were arrested on the 11th of August. Tell us how it came to be that you were arrested and tell us where you were taken.

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: As usual, I left in the morning, because a messenger had called me. I went in front of the local commune, not far away from my home. I went there for forced labour. On that day, I was given the assignment of cutting the grass in the churchyard in front of the Serb church. I worked all day, together with three or four other locals, my fellow citizens. Around 3.00, Serb soldiers came and they said that we should go home because we had completed our assignment. I got very tired that day. I went home. It was a hot day. I found a bit of water in the yard. That had been prepared by my wife. Since there was no water in the house, water was warmed in the yard, in a pot. I washed a bit and I hurried into the house to lie down, because my back had hurt from all that work, practically every day. I had not slept for 15 or 20 minutes, not more than that, and I fell asleep straight away. My wife woke me up with the following words: She said that I should get up, that Serb soldiers came to take me for an interrogation. When I went out into the hall, at the entrance door I recognised two Serbs, of Serb ethnicity, and one person whom I did not know. All three were in camouflage uniforms and armed. I knew from before, the two or three months that I had spent in the occupied Bosanski Samac, that these drivers drove a blue Lada vehicle. Whoever was taken away in that Lada never returned home again. I asked my fellow citizens, whom I knew -- one of them was Milan, from the village of Crkvina, and the other one was very familiar to me, but I did not know his name. He worked at the department store where wall-to-wall carpeting was sold. I asked them whether that meant that I was being taken away, and they said, [redacted]. Get dressed and put on some warm clothes, because you are going for some kind of an interview." Since I had just been awakened, I was still drowsy and I'd hardly dressed. I put on a T-shirt and shorts only. When I reappeared in the hall, he asked me to put on some warmer clothes, and I said, "It's the 11th of August. It's hot. I'll be hot." And he said, "Well, get dressed. You'll need it." My wife, who was listening to all of this and saw all of this and heard the entire conversation, said to them, I think, "Does that mean that my [redacted] is not going to come back?" I don't know. I was already crossing the hall, going to the room in order to listen to what they said, to wear something warmer. I heard her crying. I got dressed. I went into the hall. And I was in better shape than I am in now, and I said, "Oh, come on. Don't cry. Can't you see that these people are just taking me for an interview and I'll come back? What's with you?" I did not spend much time in the hall, and I asked them that we should get going. Their vehicle was parked on the other side of my house, that is to say, right by the heating plant, right by the heating plant that is near my house, the one that heats the apartment building. They brought me to that vehicle, and when they put me into that vehicle, I knew that there would be no return to my home. The drive from my house to the SUP building did not take long. And also, geographically speaking, we weren't far away. It's about 700 metres. But it felt so long to me. It seemed as if I'd never get there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Witness. Your expectation was that you weren't going return to your home. Did that in fact turn out to be the truth?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. It is true. I never returned home. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you -- how long were you kept in the SUP?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: I was detained in the SUP all the way up to the 27th of November, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where in the SUP were you kept?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: There was a procedure involved. When one enters the SUP, one has to leave all the things that one has in his pockets; cigarettes, house keys, money, everything. You have to leave it all. Watches. You have to leave all of that with the porter, actually, by the reception office, the first one on the left-hand side. That's where I spent the first seven days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you just general questions now about life in the SUP or conditions in the SUP. Were you beaten?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: This first room on the left-hand side, we called that the reception room, we amongst ourselves, we who were detained. And that is where the interrogation procedure takes place and also the giving of statements. I was mistreated in that room, I and three or four of my fellow citizens. On several occasions, soldiers in camouflage uniforms came and beat us, mostly during these first seven days or so.

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: [redacted], this was a man called Stojan. His last name was Blagojevic. He would come.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see your fellow prisoners being beaten?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: Yes. They beat all of us. When they would enter the room, they would beat all of us. And they had had the misfortune of being arrested before me, and they were tied up by wire. Their hands were all wounded from this wire that was tied tightly around their wrists. They were wounded black and blue over the face and body. One was called Hadzialijagic Dasa. The other was called Rukavina Igor. The third one was Hamid. He was the one who had a fish restaurant. So there were four of us, and we spent six or seven days there in this reception office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was conducting the beatings? Give us some names of men who conducted the beatings.

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: In this reception office, I was beaten by Stojan Blagojevic the most. Later, after I gave my statement -- the crime inspector upstairs, his name was Simo Bozic. I was transferred to the second office on the left-hand side of the hall. That's where I spent about ten days or so. Almost every night, Stevan Todorovic came with several Serb soldiers in uniform, and he mistreated us collectively. That is to say, he beat and mistreated all of us. Those whose names were called out individually had it the worst. I did not have that misfortune of having had my name called out individually. When a detainee would go out individually, then he would be beaten the most, and if we would go out collectively, I guess they would get tired as they beat us and not all of us would be beaten very much. In that room, there were about 15 of us detained there for about ten days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you were there until late November. Was there ever a cessation or a day -- did a day go past without yourself being beaten or other prisoners being beaten?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: No. It never happened. They always beat us, either in the morning or in the evening or very late, either collectively or they called out the names of my fellow citizens and they mistreated them. We had the opportunity of hearing all of that. That is to say, there were many days when I did not receive a single blow, but I was forced to hear the moans and wails of others who were beaten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were instruments used when the men were being beaten?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: Yes. In these beatings, they usually used various things. They hit us with their hands and with their feet in boots. They hit us with rifle butts, with sticks, with truncheons, bats. I don't know whether this was prepared for that particular purpose previously.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that wails and moans could be heard. Were these loud?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: Yes, they were, because this was three or four metres away. Everything could be heard in the SUP building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were -- I'll use this term advisedly, but when you were a free man, before you were arrested, had you ever heard any sounds coming from the SUP building or the TO building in the course of your travelling around the town, off to do your work?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: Yes [redacted]

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: [redacted]. So I often heard, while I was in the town of Samac, from the 17th of April until the 11th of August, during the night I would often hear screams and moans of people who were being beaten in these three facilities that I mentioned. It was a small town. I was a very busy man. There were many days when I was busy, but often my wife would have some time off, and when she would go to town, she would try to get hold of something at the market and then hurry back home. I don't know whether this was an assignment or not, but she would see my fellow citizens on the trucks. They were bloody, beaten, and tied up. And often she would come with news to the effect that such-and-such a person was beaten, that his teeth were pulled out, and that this particular person would be disfigured from the pain and from the blows. This made me feel afraid. When I went for my work obligation, I was kind of hoping that I be detained too, because it was so hard for me to listen to these moans from home during the night. And after the news that we received when we got back home, I was terrified, and I often weighed my options: whether it would be better to get arrested as soon as possible so that I would be with my fellow citizens, or should I continue to go to clean trenches and have a hard time that way? I was hungry and mistreated several times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You could hear screams from up [redacted] and you heard reports from your wife of bloodied figures being driven around on trucks.

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: Yes. I could hear the moans from [redacted], as the crow flies, but I didn't know at which location they were beating these people, because the elementary school gym is [redacted], the secondary school gym is [redacted], the yard of the TO building was [redacted], [redacted].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell the Chamber if --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell the Chamber if these signs and -- I'll rephrase my question. Tell the Chamber if these sorts of screams and yells that you've described could be heard throughout the period of time that you were in Bosanski Samac before your arrest, that is, from April to August, or was it a one-off incident or confined to a particular time?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: Several times during the night it used to happen, but it didn't happen every night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before I leave the SUP, I'd just like to ask you: In addition to the beatings of yourself and your fellow prisoners, were there any other forms of mistreatment that were either inflicted on you or the other men?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: Yes, there were, such as turning towards each other and slapping one another. I heard in other rooms, but I didn't take part in this, that there was also sexual mistreatment or sexual abuse between people of the same sex.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the ethnic background of the prisoners who were kept in the SUP between August and late November?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: We were all Muslims or Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you eventually leave the SUP?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: On the 27th of November, 1992, everybody in the rooms was ordered to come out into the yard of the Bosanski Samac SUP. We had the rare opportunity to go outside into the yard, and we were very happy, because I had spent the entire time in a cell intended for two persons. There were 11 of us at all times inside, without any floor covering or any conditions, without any toilet facilities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry, Witness. I forgot to ask you about that. Can you tell us -- you've already described it as being overcrowded. Were you able to at least lie down at night to sleep?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: We didn't have the opportunity, because there was no space. After ten days which I spent in another room on the left side, I was transferred to a cell across from that second room. This cell was meant for two prisoners. According to my assessment - and I can't remember precisely - by the end of August, I was already in that cell, detained with 11 of my fellow citizens. I spent the entire time there without a coat, without a blanket, without water, without a toilet, in an area of 9 square metres, all that time until the 27th of November. We had the possibility to go to the toilet, but there was no water in the toilet, and we could do this after asking the guard who was standing in the corridor. So that means that we had to open the door, greet the guard, and then ask whether we would be allowed to use the toilet. Each person on duty took care that we did not go to the toilet several times, so we avoided going to the toilet, because he used to come after my fellow citizens, the person on duty, or a fighter from the Serbian army, and beat up that fellow citizen who happened to go to the toilet. He would come back all bloody and in bruises, and he would tell us why he was in that state, so that we avoided going to the toilet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us about the food that you received in the time that you were kept in the SUP.

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: Food was brought by a Serbian soldier in a van. Initially, during the first 15 days, I had the opportunity to see that through the window, because I was on the left side of the SUP building. It was brought in a van. One or two prisoners would quickly run out when the guard would order them to go out. They would go out and take the food. Usually we would get one kilogramme of bread, to be distributed amongst 20 or 25 people, and this would be sometime between 1.00 and 1.30 p.m. And we would get a little bit of tea, which was hardly enough to fill a soldier's ration. And this is what we would receive once every 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I started to ask you about your departure from the SUP. Can I ask you to return to that topic? When did you leave the SUP, and under what circumstances did that occur?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: I left the SUP after the command, "Go out," and I think this happened during my two or three months' stay there, that we would go outside on two or three other occasions. Then on those occasions we would go out to the SUP yard, which was facing the Sava River. And we tried to stretch our legs as much as possible, because we didn't have the opportunity to do that in the cell. However, the commander of the police station appeared. This is how he introduced himself, by the name of Stoko. I think that he said that he worked at the Orasje police station before the war. He ordered us to tie white ribbons or bands around our eyes, around our heads, which were distributed by Serbian soldiers. So we received blindfolds. People were there in the yard also from the TO building, and also I think that people came from the secondary school, people who were detained in the gym there. According to my estimate, there were about 150 of us there. All of us were loaded into three buses, wearing blindfolds, and these buses were full. They were parked right next to the yard, the SUP building yard. We were issued with the command to put the blindfolds on and to go into the buses, and we obeyed this order. We went into the buses with the help of the Serbian soldiers who most probably, as far as I can remember and as far as my ears can serve me because I wasn't able to look, they were counting us and loading us into those buses. I heard the sound of those trucks, those buses when the engines were turned on. We travelled for a long time in a direction that I didn't know. At several points, I heard the conversation of Serbian soldiers who were in the buses -- in the bus. I guess they were accompanying us. And I also heard the men who were manning the checkpoints, "Who are these people who are inside? Where are they going and why are they going?" at the checkpoints, it was often said, the checkpoints in my town of Samac. Later, I would hear that I arrived at the village of Batkovici, which is at the place where the River Drina flows into the River Sava.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: So later, I would hear that this is where I arrived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Thank you. Thank you for describing that. Can you just give us a date, if you can, please, or at least an approximate time when you were transferred from SUP to the Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: Later in the afternoon. According to my estimate, it could have been 4.00 or 4.30 in the afternoon on the 27th of November, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, how long did you remain at Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: From that date until the 4th of October, 1994.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you detained in Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: In the hangar of the Pik agriculture cooperative. Pik Semberija. I think that's what it's called.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how many men were kept there with you in that period of time?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: There were two hangars full of men. According to my estimate, because I had plenty of months to figure out its size, it was 26 by 50, and at certain points there were even 700 of us who were detained there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You endured that place for close on two years. Were most of the men who were kept there from Bosanski Samac or were they men who came in from different parts of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: According to my estimate, there were about 150 of my fellow citizens there, while the others were from Srebrenica, from the town of Tuzla, from the town of Prijedor, from the town of Kozarac, and from the town of Kljuc, because that is what they told me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the ethnic background of the men who were imprisoned with you?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: We were all Serbs [as interpreted] and Croats except for -- on a couple of occasions for those who were arrested at the lines. To this very day, I cannot come to a proper conclusion, but when they captured a large number of people, they would bring them here so that on a couple of occasions, people of Serb ethnicity were also brought there who were captured during attacks on some territories.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. di Fazio, can we look at the first line of the answer? "We were all Serbs and Croats." Maybe we could have a clarification. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. I'm just about to do that. I'm grateful to Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Okay. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you just-- your first answer -- sorry. In the previous answer you said, and I quote from the transcript that I see, "We were all Serbs and Croats except for -- on a couple of occasions for those who were arrested at the lines." Is that what you meant to say?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: No, that is not what I meant to say. My real proper answer should have said, "Muslims and Croats."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did anyone ever explain to you, either at the SUP or in Batkovic, what it was that you'd done wrong to cause this imprisonment of yours?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: Around the beginning of 1993, material most probably came from my municipality, the municipality of the town of Samac, and it was an indictment by Serb soldiers against me so that court proceedings were initiated, so that I and a couple of my other fellow citizens were taken by a vehicle. And this happened on several occasions. I was taken for trial to the military court in the town of Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the accusation levelled against you?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: The charges were that we wanted to kill and occupy the Serbian people which were in favour of life together. They were nice. They were good. They were our fellow citizens, and we wanted to occupy them with those weapons that I received on the 16th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. I see. Did the charge somehow relate to the gun that you'd been given at the TO? Is that your understanding of the accusation? That's what I'd like to know.

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That is what I was told. And I told them, just as I have told you now. I said everything from A to Z in the courtroom and during my questioning, that I received a rifle on the 16th, held onto it for 16 hours and returned it to a Serbian soldier. I was and tried to remain an honourable citizen of Bosanski Samac, but I don't know how much I succeeded in that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the result of this trial that you underwent in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: The result in Bijeljina was three and a half years' imprisonment because of aggression against the Serbian people and Serbian territory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have a lawyer?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: I did have a lawyer who was assigned to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have a chance to speak to him and did he assist you to deny the charges?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: I didn't have the opportunity, and I noticed, since we spoke in the same language, we understood one another very well, my attorney, the one assigned to me, was more against me than in favour of me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you got any idea when you received this sentence of three and a half years, at what point of time?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: Sometime in the month of February or March 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to ask you briefly about conditions in Batkovic in the two years or so that you were there. Were there beatings?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: Yes. They often beat us. I say "often" because up until before the war, I wasn't used to being beaten by my parents, and I wasn't used to it as a way of upbringing or correction. So it would be for 15 or 20 blows. But we were taken out for forced labour. Also they would come to the hangar and beat us collectively and individually. I did not have the opportunity, the misfortune, of being individually beaten. However, on several occasions I had the opportunity, after just being woken up from sleep, at 2.00 or 3.00 a.m., to be ordered to turn around to the first person sleeping next to me, so that we would slap one another, and we would have to slap one another in the presence of Serbian soldiers. Those who did not comply were hit on the knuckles with a rifle butt. I also was present during individual beatings of my fellow citizens, and this was very difficult for me to see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Just a clarification here. In Batkovic, after you had been sentenced, were you beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before that and after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: Would Your Honours just bear with me, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber if the frequency of beating at Batkovic was different from that of the SUP? And in general, can you tell the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Chamber if there was any difference in the conditions in Batkovic and the SUP?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: Yes, there were conditions, if you can call it that way. We were overcrowded inside during the first few weeks of my detention in Batkovic. I didn't have clothes on me, because the clothes that I was wearing when I left my house were torn by the 13th of December, 1992. No one helped me by giving me any kind of clothing. The clothes that I was wearing were in tatters. So until that date that I mentioned earlier, then the Red Cross for the first time to register me. According to what they said - and I didn't know what this meant - they tried to calm us down by saying we were safe now, that we could not be liquidated. The conditions were before the 27th of November. We arrived around 8.00 in the evening to the hangars in Batkovic. They ordered us to take our blindfolds off. In front of me there was a wire fence, a line of Serbian soldiers wearing probably Serbian camouflage units [as interpreted], and we were supposed to run this gauntlet from the bus to the gate. We were beaten with rifle butts on our backs, on our shoulders, and we were ordered to move faster. When we arrived in the yard of the building, which was surrounded by a wire fence which, according to my estimate, was about two and a half metres high, and I did have enough time to register that -- when I left the hangar, I could see two guard houses in front of me, observation towers, and there would always be a soldier in a camouflage uniform with a rifle at the ready towards the gate where we would go out. The yard building was very large. When we would go outside, we had space to stretch our legs and to walk around, and that was what they had ordered us to do. Most probably we would have remained fit -- this was done most probably so that we would keep fit. The conditions there were slightly better. We received a meal twice a day, which was not sufficient, since we kept going out for work day in and day out. Fifty soldiers -- fifty inmates would go to Panafleks, fifty would go to Hranaprodukt, fifty would go to the fields, fifty would go to gather the corn. So that sometimes we were not all taken out, so those who remained in the hangar would not be permitted to go out and to move. And those lucky ones - and I say lucky ones - who would go out to work, did have, really, they did have better food, and we were anxious and we fought to get onto that list. The list was compiled by a man who slept at the hangar with us. Sometimes it was a Croat or sometimes it was a Muslim, and we would beg him to put us on the list. On that day when fewer workers were required, we would be very sad, because the majority would remain hungry in the hangars.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I'd just like you to now just list for the Chamber the sorts of labour that you did in Batkovic. I don't need to know all the details, but just give us a general, quick description of the sort of work that you did in the time that you were there.

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: I was digging the next year, so it was in the spring of 1993. I planted in the fields, I cultivated the fields, and I gathered into burlap sacks wheat which had been harvested the year before. I went to the forest to cut wood. I went out into the field for two or three days to Majevica, to dig trenches, and then again to the line of separation between the B and H army and the Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you do much work on trenches in the two years that you were in custody at Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: No. I wasn't assigned to trench digging very much, but when I was taken to Majevica - the exact location is Piperi - that is where I was digging the trenches and that is where we used to sleep also, in a school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just answer me briefly, if you can: Did you ever have the hope of being exchanged?

utterances.speaker: The permit that you obtained, was it a multiple entry/exit
utterances.text: Yes. I hoped each time when the gate to the hangar would open. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, it's 5.00 now, and you may have gathered I'm getting very close to the end of my examination-in-chief. I'll certainly complete it fairly quickly in the morning, and it's a new topic. Would this be an appropriate time to break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Before we break, I did announce earlier that we would sit up to Thursday afternoon. I've been informed that because of the diplomatic meeting in the gallery, the technical people will not use the -- we will need to use the equipment from the courtroom, so that we wouldn't be able to have the equipment with us if we were to sit in the afternoon. So tomorrow we will sit up to 1.00, and the next proceedings will be Monday next week. So the Court will rise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 22nd day of November, 2001, at 9.30 a.m. 25
